title: The Forty-Seven Ronin
text:
In the spring of 1701, inside the shogun's castle at Edo, the young lord Asano Naganori of Ako drew his sword and wounded Kira Yoshinaka, a senior court official. Drawing a blade in the castle was a grave crime. Asano was ordered to commit suicide the same day, his domain was confiscated, and his samurai became ronin, masterless men. Kira was not punished.

Asano's chief retainer, Oishi Kuranosuke, first tried to have the house restored under Asano's brother. When that failed, he and a group of former retainers committed themselves to avenging their lord. They scattered, took humble work, and waited, so that Kira's guards would lower their watch. Later tradition says Oishi lived a dissolute life in Kyoto to throw off suspicion.

On a snowy night at the end of 1702 by the Japanese calendar (early 1703 in ours), forty-seven of them stormed Kira's mansion in Edo. They found him hiding, killed him, and carried his head to their lord's grave at Sengaku-ji temple. Then they turned themselves in to the authorities.

The shogunate debated what to do with men who had broken the law out of loyalty. In early 1703 it ordered the forty-six who had surrendered to commit seppuku, which they did. They were buried beside Asano at Sengaku-ji, where visitors still burn incense at their graves. Their story became the basis of Chushingura, one of Japan's most performed plays.
lesson: A group that shares one purpose can stay united for years without visible progress. Patience and discretion are often what make collective commitment succeed.
people: Oishi Kuranosuke, Asano Naganori, Kira Yoshinaka, the Ako ronin
source: Contemporary records of the Ako incident; Takeda Izumo and others, Kanadehon Chushingura (1748)
caveat: Many details popular today, such as Oishi's feigned debauchery, come from later drama rather than contemporary records.
